angleCategories.name: Offer & Incentive
angleCategories.psychology: Give someone a compelling reason to act
angleCategories.concept: Give the customer a tangible reason to take action: an attractive offer, introductory incentive, trial, complimentary service, or clearly defined package. Valuable, specific, easy to understand.
rules: Lead with the actual offer.
Include the price or financial incentive when relevant.
Clearly explain what is included.
Highlight any legitimate limitations or eligibility requirements.
Don't invent discounts, free services, or promotional deadlines.
angleCategories.formats: Offer-led static image, short promotional video, package comparison carousel, or service demonstration with an offer overlay.
examples: Your first class is on us.

angleCategories.name: Transformation & Results
angleCategories.concept: Help the customer visualize the result of buying. Demonstrate the value rather than describing it.
rules: Prioritize actual client, customer, or product results.
Use before-and-after creative when suitable and platform-compliant.
Include specific outcomes only when documented.
Avoid suggesting every customer will experience the same result.
When a physical transformation isn't appropriate, use a customer success story.
angleCategories.formats: Before-and-after carousel, transformation Reel, case-study video, comparison imagery, or customer story.
examples: Two hours completely transformed this driveway.
You won't believe this is the same car.
Wait until you see this pup after their appointment.

angleCategories.name: Social Proof
angleCategories.psychology: Show that other people trust the business
angleCategories.concept: Let satisfied customers communicate the value and credibility of the business.
rules: Use authentic testimonials, reviews, or case studies.
Include verifiable ratings, review counts, and customer results.
Prioritize relatable customer experiences.
Don't manufacture testimonials, numbers, or endorsement claims.
Select proof relevant to the service being advertised.
angleCategories.formats: UGC, testimonial video, review overlays, case-study carousel, customer reaction footage.
examples: See why homeowners across [City] choose our team.
Don't take our word for it. Meet our members.
Here's why these pet parents keep coming back.

angleCategories.name: Education & Myth Busting
angleCategories.concept: Answer the questions customers have before purchasing and help them understand the product or service.
rules: Identify common customer questions, concerns, or misconceptions.
Lead with one specific question.
Provide genuinely useful information.
Keep the language simple and conversational.
Present the business as a knowledgeable resource.
Don't exaggerate risks, invent facts, or make unsupported health or financial claims.
angleCategories.formats: Expert talking-head video, FAQ carousel, myth-versus-fact graphic, whiteboard explanation, or demonstration.
examples: What actually happens during your first Botox appointment?
Three signs your AC might need servicing.
How often should your dog actually be groomed?

angleCategories.name: Process & Demonstration
angleCategories.psychology: Show the product or service in action
angleCategories.concept: Show the customer what happens when they buy, visit, book, or use the service. Let people watch it.
rules: Focus on one visually interesting process.
Show real products, team members, tools, or service delivery.
Use close-up footage when applicable.
Explain what the viewer is watching.
Keep the content natural rather than overly polished.
Use hooks that create curiosity.
angleCategories.formats: POV footage, behind-the-scenes video, ASMR-style footage, short demonstrations, process montages, and walkthroughs.
examples: Come behind the scenes of a HydraFacial appointment.
Here's what 45 minutes at [Studio] actually looks like.
30 seconds of the most satisfying car detail you'll see today.

angleCategories.name: Authority & Trust
angleCategories.concept: Why choose this business instead of another: credibility, expertise, transparency, professionalism, and the real people behind it.
rules: Identify the business's strongest genuine differentiator.
Show the owner, specialist, team, or facilities.
Highlight relevant qualifications, experience, certifications, and achievements.
Use local credibility when applicable.
Avoid vague claims such as "the best in town" without substantiation.
Prioritize specific proof over generic statements.
angleCategories.formats: Business owner talking-head video, team introductions, clinic or facility tour, local project montage, documentary-style footage.
examples: I'm Dr. [Name], and here's what you can expect at our practice.
Meet the team taking care of homes across [City].
I'm [Name], and here's what makes our studio different.

angleCategories.name: Problem & Solution
angleCategories.psychology: Connect an existing problem to a solution
angleCategories.concept: Highlight a specific problem customers already recognize, then introduce the business as a relevant solution. Specific and practical, not exaggerated fear.
rules: Identify a realistic customer problem.
Show how it affects their life or creates inconvenience.
Introduce the service as a possible solution.
Explain what the business actually does.
End with a logical next step.
Avoid fearmongering, personal-attribute assumptions, or guaranteed outcomes.
angleCategories.formats: Problem/solution video, UGC-style talking head, simple comparison graphic, educational carousel.
examples: That strange noise coming from your AC might be worth checking.
Not all roof damage is obvious from the ground.
When a quick car wash just isn't cutting it.

angleCategories.name: Seasonal & Urgency
angleCategories.psychology: Create timely, legitimate reasons to act
angleCategories.concept: Connect the offer to a relevant time, season, event, deadline, or real availability limit, so the customer has a reason to act now.
rules: Identify real seasonal or event-based demand.
Make the context geographically relevant where needed.
Only include genuine deadlines, inventory constraints, or booking limitations.
Avoid fabricated scarcity.
Connect the event or season to a specific offer or service.
angleCategories.formats: Promotional Reel, deadline-led static, seasonal service video, collection teaser, event announcement.
examples: Get your AC serviced before the summer heat arrives.
Game day plans? We've got your food covered.

angleCategories.name: Convenience & Accessibility
angleCategories.concept: Show how the business removes time, effort, uncertainty, or friction from buying. This angle sells simplicity.
rules: Identify what makes purchasing or booking easier.
Emphasize genuine conveniences such as location, scheduling, mobile service, delivery, payment options, or a simplified process.
Focus on one primary convenience per ad.
Make the next step immediately clear.
Never invent financing terms, service speeds, or availability.
angleCategories.formats: POV videos, booking walkthroughs, convenience-focused talking heads, simple graphics, day-in-the-life footage.
examples: Professional car detailing, right in your driveway.
Morning, midday, or evening. Find a class that fits your schedule.
Your dog's grooming appointment, right outside your front door.

angleCategories.name: Product & Service Showcase
angleCategories.concept: Make the product, service, location, or experience the hero. Lead with what makes the offering desirable.
rules: Highlight one hero product or service.
Show the offering in its best authentic setting.
Emphasize tangible features and differentiators.
Include product or service details that help the customer make a decision.
Prioritize real visuals over generic stock imagery.
angleCategories.formats: Product videos, cinematic close-ups, lifestyle imagery, service showcases, carousels, walkthroughs, and collection videos.
examples: This is our best-selling dish, and it's easy to see why.
Meet the piece we're known for.
Come take a closer look at our HydraFacial treatment.

generalNiche.label: this kind of business
generalNiche.form_fields: Name, phone, what they're interested in

headlineStructures.name: Direct offer
headlineStructures.use: Straight to the point. Excellent for lead generation when the business has a strong offer.
headlineStructures.rule: Lead with the offer. Don't bury the price or incentive behind clever wording.

headlineStructures.name: Freebie
headlineStructures.use: When the business offers something complimentary that lowers the barrier to becoming a lead.
headlineStructures.rule: Be specific about what is free. Only use this structure when the offer is genuinely complimentary.

headlineStructures.name: Desired outcome
headlineStructures.use: Focuses on what the customer wants rather than the technical details of the service.
headlineStructures.rule: Focus on a tangible outcome. Don't promise results that the business cannot guarantee.
examples: A Fresh Look for Your Driveway
A Fresh Look for Your Home

headlineStructures.name: Curiosity
headlineStructures.structure: [Question or intriguing statement related to the service]
headlineStructures.use: Gives someone a reason to click and learn more.
headlineStructures.rule: Create curiosity without withholding essential information or resorting to clickbait.
examples: Looking for Your Next Favorite Gym?

headlineStructures.name: Problem / solution
headlineStructures.use: Connects a common frustration directly to the service.
headlineStructures.rule: Focus on everyday problems. Don't use aggressive fear-based messaging or imply knowledge of someone's sensitive personal circumstances.
examples: AC Not Working? Book a Visit.
No Time to Cook? Order Online.
Need a New Roof? Get a Quote.

headlineStructures.name: Social proof
headlineStructures.use: Uses genuine credibility to reinforce the decision.
headlineStructures.rule: Numerical claims must come from verified business information. Never invent ratings, reviews, testimonials, or results.
examples: See Why Our Members Love Us

headlineStructures.name: Location
headlineStructures.use: Makes an ad feel immediately relevant to someone in the service area.
headlineStructures.rule: Use the business's actual service area. Location-specific headlines should sound natural rather than like keyword-stuffed search ads.
examples: Your New Favorite Miami Brunch Spot

headlineStructures.name: Urgency
headlineStructures.use: Gives prospective customers a timely reason to act.
headlineStructures.rule: Urgency must be genuine. Never invent a deadline, claim limited availability without confirmation, or manufacture scarcity.
examples: Last Week of Our Spring Special

headlineStructures.name: Convenience
headlineStructures.use: Sells the ease of working with the business.
headlineStructures.rule: Highlight genuine conveniences, such as mobile service, flexible appointments, easy booking, or delivery.

headlineStructures.name: Showcase
headlineStructures.use: Works when the product or creative itself is the main selling point.
headlineStructures.rule: Highlight the most interesting or desirable aspect of the offering. Avoid generic headlines such as "Discover Our Services" when a more specific alternative exists.
examples: Take a Look Inside Our Studio

headlineStructures.name: Benefit stack
headlineStructures.use: Communicates multiple selling points in a compact, scannable format.
headlineStructures.rule: Use two or three complementary benefits. Prioritize clarity over cleverness.

headlineStructures.name: Direct action
headlineStructures.use: A straightforward conversion-focused headline that tells the customer exactly what to do.
headlineStructures.rule: Align the action with the actual conversion destination. Don't instruct someone to book if the next step is only a consultation request or information form.

creativeTypes.name: Experience and lifestyle
creativeTypes.communicates: What buying or booking feels like

restaurant.direction: Make the food the hero. Prioritize mouthwatering close-ups, movement, texture, and authentic kitchen footage over polished graphics.
prioritize: Food preparation videos: stretching dough, pouring coffee, plating dishes, sizzling food.
Close-up hero shots: cheese pulls, steam, drizzling sauces, fresh ingredients.
Deal-led creative: an appetizing photo with a large, easy-to-read offer.
Customer review overlays on real restaurant or food footage.
Location awareness: the exterior, recognizable surroundings, and food.
Occasion-based creative: date nights, game days, brunch, late-night dining.
restaurant.example: A 15-second Reel opening with a pizza coming out of the oven, then a cheese pull, with the offer as the overlay.
restaurant.avoid: Generic stock food photos, text-heavy menus, wide food shots, and creative where you can't immediately tell what's being sold.

real_estate.direction: Sell the property, lifestyle, or local expertise. Show real listings and use video to bring properties to life.
prioritize: Property carousels featuring the best rooms and outdoor spaces.
Walkthrough videos using natural phone footage.
A strong hero image with clear property information, including price where appropriate.
Home valuation creative featuring recognizable local neighborhoods.
Agent talking-head videos explaining the market.
Sold-property case studies with actual transaction results.
real_estate.example: A 30-second walkthrough of the kitchen, living area, backyard and exterior with a simple "Just Listed in [City]" opening.
real_estate.avoid: Luxury photos unrelated to the listing, cluttered property graphics, unsupported statistics, and hiding important property details.
real_estate.compliance: Real estate campaigns must follow housing advertising and targeting requirements.

home_services.direction: Make the transformation instantly obvious. Customers should understand what the business does and why it's valuable within seconds.
prioritize: Before-and-after carousels: a strong starting format for visible services.
Satisfying service videos: pressure washing, painting, deep cleaning, landscaping.
Seasonal offers tied to real demand, like AC maintenance before summer.
Real team members working at real job sites.
Genuine Google review overlays.
Trust signals like licensed and insured, where true.
home_services.example: A 4-card carousel: dirty driveway, cleaned driveway, close-up of the result, team photo with "Get a Free Quote."
home_services.avoid: Stock photos of technicians, unclear before and afters, generic graphics that don't show the work, and burying the offer under text.

med_spa.direction: Combine visual appeal with trust. Show the treatment experience, the clinic's professionalism, and the value of booking.
prioritize: Process videos: close-up treatment footage is naturally engaging and a strong first test.
Before-and-after imagery, only where consented, substantiated and allowed by Meta.
First-time offer creative with clear introductory pricing.
Clinic footage: clean treatment rooms, modern equipment, professional surroundings.
Real client testimonial videos.
Practitioner introductions explaining what happens during a treatment.
med_spa.example: A 15-second treatment video, then a shot of the treatment room, ending on the offer as the overlay.
med_spa.avoid: Overly retouched results, generic beauty stock photos, too much text, invasive procedure imagery, or anything implying the viewer has an appearance insecurity.

fitness.direction: Sell the experience, not the equipment. People should be able to picture themselves in a class, enjoying it.
prioritize: Real class footage: energy, movement, instructors and members.
Community videos with genuine interactions.
Free trial offer creative.
Trainer talking-head videos introducing the studio.
Real member testimonials and progress stories.
Facility walkthroughs for first-time visitors.
fitness.example: A fast montage of a group class, the instructor coaching and members interacting, ending on the offer.
fitness.avoid: Empty equipment photos, intimidating stock fitness models, unrealistic transformation promises, and aggressive motivational messages.

roofing.direction: Combine visible roof condition, inspection footage and strong local credibility.
prioritize: Drone footage of real roofs and inspection areas.
Close-ups of documented storm damage.
Before-and-after roof replacement carousels.
Local crews completing installations.
Free inspection offers.
Trust signals: verified licensing, insurance, warranty, completed local projects.
roofing.example: A drone video of a roof inspection with the overlay "Recent Storms in [City]? Book a Roof Inspection."
roofing.avoid: Generic disaster imagery, exaggerated damage, made-up storms, and unconditional "$0 out of pocket" insurance promises.

clothing.direction: Make the product desirable in a real-world context. Show real people wearing it, not only studio photos.
prioritize: UGC try-on videos with real customers or creators.
Styling videos showing several ways to wear one piece.
Best-selling product close-ups.
Collection carousels worn by real people.
Unboxing and first-impression videos.
Real restock announcements and new collection previews.
clothing.example: A creator's casual mirror try-on with the overlay "3 Ways I'd Style Our Best-Selling Set."
clothing.avoid: Only flat lays, too much studio polish, complicated collages, and visuals that hide the fit.

dental.direction: Build trust while making treatment feel understandable and approachable. Prioritize real, dentist-led content.
prioritize: Dentist talking-head videos explaining procedures simply.
Genuine patient testimonials with authorization.
Consented patient results, where Meta allows.
Clinic walkthroughs: modern equipment, a welcoming space.
Consultation offer creative.
Educational videos answering treatment questions and payment options.
dental.example: The dentist to camera: "Thinking about dental implants? Here's what actually happens at your first consultation."
dental.avoid: Disturbing procedure footage, unsupported medical claims, exaggerated outcomes, and unverified financing promises.

chiro.direction: Make the practitioner familiar and the treatment easy to understand. Use real clinic footage and education.
prioritize: The chiropractor talking directly to camera.
Short appointment process videos.
First-visit walkthroughs.
Clinic introductions with the practitioner and the space.
Educational clips: exercises or common questions.
Real patient testimonials, with authorization and appropriate claims.
chiro.example: A 20-second video, "What Happens at Your First Chiropractic Appointment?", showing the consultation and each step.
chiro.avoid: Sensational cracking videos as the whole strategy, medical promises, fear-based messages, and diagnosing the viewer.

auto_detailing.direction: Lean into satisfying, visual footage. This service naturally produces strong creative.
prioritize: Dramatic vehicle before-and-after shots.
ASMR-style detailing: pressure washing, foam cannons, polishing.
Ceramic coating demos showing water beading.
Interior deep-clean transformations.
Package showcase videos.
Mobile detailing footage arriving at the customer's place.
auto_detailing.example: A 15-second montage: dirty interior, extraction, steam cleaning, finished result, with the package as the overlay.
auto_detailing.avoid: Luxury car photos without real service footage, heavy effects that hide the results, and cars that aren't their work.

pest.direction: Make professional pest control look reliable, approachable and easy to arrange.
prioritize: Technicians inspecting real properties.
Seasonal educational videos about common local pests.
Simple service-process explainers.
Free inspection offer graphics.
Real customer reviews.
Trust content: uniforms, vehicles, equipment, team members.
pest.example: A technician walking around a home explaining three places they check during a routine inspection.
pest.avoid: Graphic pest imagery, exaggerated infestations, unsupported safety claims, and spraying footage with no context.

pet.direction: Make the animals the stars, with reassurance about the quality of care.
prioritize: Before-and-after grooming transformations.
Satisfying grooming process videos.
Happy pets comfortable with the groomers.
Groomer introductions.
First-time customer offers.
Mobile grooming demos or salon walkthroughs.
pet.example: A short Reel: a fluffy dog walks in, ends on the finished groom, overlay "Fresh Cut. Happy Pup."
pet.avoid: Stock pet photos, distressed animals, forced reactions, and heavy graphics that distract from the animals.

rulebook.label: Watch
rulebook.rule: Don't judge an ad until it has run 3 days and spent about 2 times the target cost per lead. If it's between the target and 2 times the target, give it 2 to 3 more days.

rulebook.label: Kill
rulebook.rule: Turn off an ad that has spent 2 times the target with no leads, or costs more than 2 times the target after spending 3 times the target.

rulebook.label: Scale
rulebook.rule: At or under the target: leave it alone. After 5 or more days under the target, raise the budget 20%, then wait 3 days before raising it again. If the cost jumps after a raise, go back to the last budget.

rulebook.label: Refresh
rulebook.rule: When people have seen it more than 3 times on average, or clicks have dropped by about a third, add 2 or 3 new ads. Leave the old ones running.

rulebook.label: Never
rulebook.rule: Judge an ad in its first 24 hours, double the budget, or edit an ad that's working (make a new one instead).

rulebook.label: No target yet
rulebook.rule: If the client has no target cost per lead, the first 2 weeks set the baseline.

diagnosis.sign: Expensive to show and few clicks
diagnosis.meaning: The creative isn't stopping the scroll. Add new ads with different angles and visuals.
The form, page or offer is the problem. Check it on a phone, shorten the form, make the offer clearer.
Follow-up. Leads need a call or text within 5 minutes. This is the client's side: show them the numbers.
Sales. The ads are doing their job. Show the client the booked numbers and talk about the consultation.

generalAdRules: No fake reviews, results, testimonials, credentials or scarcity.
Don't call out personal traits in the ad ("Are you overweight?", "Struggling with acne?"). Meta rejects these.
The ad and the page or form after the click must say the same thing.
healthAdRules: Before and after photos: never for weight loss. For cosmetic treatments, only the business's own real results with the client's written permission, and check Meta's current health and wellness ad policy first.
No promises about how someone will look ("Look 10 years younger", "Fix your wrinkles").
No drug brand names, body or scale imagery for weight loss offers.
Lead with the offer and the experience, with confident, warm language.
Use real photos of the providers and the space where possible.
Exclude existing clients if the business has a customer list.

promptText.knowledge:
STRATEGY KNOWLEDGE (use as guidance, not rigid rules)
- Local businesses: broad targeting around the business, mention the city, lead with a specific offer. Leads usually go to a Meta Instant Form with 2 or 3 qualifying questions. Speed to lead matters: follow up within 5 minutes.
- Med spas and aesthetics: offer-first creative, real provider photos, confident language. Lead forms preferred.
- Dental: routine and cosmetic offers should be separate campaigns. Routine: team and family imagery. Cosmetic: aspirational imagery, consultation offer.
- Weight loss and GLP-1: program-focused, warm and non-judgmental, no body or scale imagery, no drug names, no guarantees.
- Online stores: send people straight to the exact product page. UGC style (real people, phone-shot) usually beats polished creative. Start with bestsellers.
- Coaching and courses: pain-led, transformation-led and credibility-led angles are worth testing. Video helps for higher-priced offers.
- Professional services and B2B: outcome-led, peer-to-peer tone.
- Universal: don't spread a small budget across many ads. Match the ad to the page or form after the click.
promptText.honesty:
HONESTY RULES (these win over everything)
- Never invent facts, offers, prices, discounts, reviews, ratings, review counts, results, credentials, years in business, customer counts, scarcity or deadlines. Use only what is in THE BUSINESS and THEIR WEBSITE above. If you suggest an offer, say it's a suggestion in assumptions.
- When the strongest version of a line needs a fact you don't have, write a short blank in square brackets instead, like [price], [regular price], [Google rating], [number of reviews], [years in business], [provider name], [end date]. The freelancer fills these in with the client. Never put a made-up value in its place. Use at most 3 blanks per ad.
- No guarantees. No numbers for expected leads, sales, cost per lead or return.
- No em dashes or en dashes. No hashtags.
- The strategy, setup, journey, launch and "why" fields are written to the freelancer (a beginner), in plain words. Explain any ad term in a few words the first time.
promptText.adCopyStyle:
HOW TO WRITE THE ADS (direct, local, specific)
These ads are written by the business to its customers. Write like the best-performing local business ads on Facebook and Instagram:
- The first line does the most work. Lead with the offer, the result, or the most interesting specific thing, following the angle. A scroller should know what this is and why it's worth a look from line one.
- Short lines. One idea per line. Line breaks between lines are good.
- Be specific: the actual treatment, dish, service, price, time, place. Name the city or area when it helps.
- Say what they get and why this business, in plain words.
- One trust line using real facts (or a [blank] for the client to fill), like "[Google rating] from [number of reviews] reviews" or "Licensed and insured" only if provided.
- End with one clear next step that matches the button.
- 30 to 80 words of primary text in total.
- Headlines: under 40 characters, specific and concrete, written in the headline structures given for each angle. Title Case like the examples.

Don't:
- Open with a vague or soft question ("Not sure which facial to choose?", "Feeling overwhelmed?").
- Use filler or spa-brochure language ("we take the time to", "on your journey", "elevate", "pamper yourself", "navigate the options").
- Describe feelings in general terms when you could name the actual thing.
- Assume something about the reader's body, health, age or appearance ("Struggling with acne?").

Bad headline: "Not sure which facial to choose"
Good headline: "Your first HydraFacial, [price]"
Bad first line: "You are looking for a facial but feel overwhelmed by all the different options available."
Good first line: "Your first facial at [Business], [price] (usually [regular price])."
promptText.angleGuide:
EACH ANGLE BECOMES ONE FINISHED AD. Fill these parts:
- category: the angle category id (like ANG-01).
- name: the angle name.
- why: one sentence to the freelancer on why this angle fits this business.
- format: the best ad format for it (like "Single image", "Before and after carousel", "Short vertical video (Reels)", "Talking-head video"), based on the angle and the creative they have.
- hooks: exactly 3 different first lines for the ad. Each a genuinely different way in: one leading with the offer or result, one leading with something specific or local, one leading with a question that names the actual thing. Under 20 words each.
- headlines: exactly 6, two different headlines in each of the three headline structures listed for that angle, in that order. structure = the structure id (like HL-01), text = the headline, under 40 characters. If a structure needs a fact you don't have (a price, a rating, a real deadline), use a [blank]. If the offer isn't genuinely free, write the Freebie headline about the free first step only if one exists; otherwise use HL-12 Direct action instead and set structure to HL-12.
- bodies: exactly 2 short middles (1 to 3 short lines, under 45 words) that follow the hook. The first focuses on what they get. The second focuses on why choose this business. Don't repeat the hook.
- trust_line: one short line of proof from real facts, or with a [blank] (like "[Google rating] stars from [number of reviews] local reviews"). Empty string only if no kind of proof makes sense.
- next_step: one short line telling them what to do, matching the button.
- description: under 30 characters, shown under the headline.
- image: the creative for this ad, following the CREATIVE DIRECTION and CREATIVE TYPES.
  creative_type: the creative type id (like CR-03).
  visual: one or two sentences describing the finished creative, like the niche example (what it opens on, what it shows, what it ends on).
  shots: 3 to 5 specific things the business should film or photograph for it, using their real business, team and work (like "Close-up of the facial being applied, 5 seconds"). Never stock.
  overlay: text on the image or final frame, under 8 words, may include a [blank].
  prompt: a detailed prompt for ChatGPT to make a stand-in image only if they have no real photo. No text in the image, no before and after, no real people's faces implied as customers, square 1:1.
- video: a short Reels idea the business can film on a phone: title, and a script under 60 words with what to show and say. Especially for process, demonstration and talking-head angles.

copyVoice:
Conversational expert copy"

Pasted by Suzy on 2026-10-11 as the voice for all copy the tools write.
Note for the Ads tool: the original is written for a marketer talking to a business owner.
In client ads, the "expert" becomes the business (owner or provider) talking to its own customer.

Conversational expert copy
Write copy that sounds like a very smart marketer talking directly to a business owner on a call.
They know the market. They have seen the problem before. They are explaining what they genuinely think in clear, natural language.
The voice should feel human and conversational, but not overly casual.
Think: experienced expert speaking naturally
NOT: copywriter writing an ad
NOT: friend chatting on FaceTime
NOT: corporate consultant presenting a recommendation
The writing should feel like something the client could actually hear you say on a strategy call.

## Inputs
Before writing, use the information provided in the prompt or conversation to understand:
1. The business, offer, product, or service.
2. The target customer or segment.
3. The customer's actual problems, situations, objections, priorities, and language.
4. The angle or idea being explored.
5. Any facts, proof, examples, numbers, or claims that are explicitly provided.
6. Any vocabulary, terminology, or wording preferences provided.

Only use factual claims, proof, numbers, guarantees, or offer details that have actually been provided.
Never invent: statistics, results, customer quotes, testimonials, features, offer details, guarantees, proof, business circumstances presented as fact.
If something has not been provided, do not manufacture it to make the copy stronger.

## The central rule
Do not try to make the copy sound impressive.
Start with the most useful or interesting observation you would naturally make if the business owner described this situation to you.
Let the insight carry the copy. The sentence itself can be simple.
Too written: "Cheap leads are expensive."
Better: "A low cost per lead does not mean much if those leads are not turning into appointments."
Better still when the situation supports it: "If your cost per lead looks great but hardly any of those people are booking, I would not increase the ad budget yet."
The third version contains judgment. It sounds like an experienced person actually responding to the situation.

## Voice
Should be: conversational, intelligent, calm, direct, specific, confident without being absolute, observant, practical, human, easy to follow, naturally opinionated when appropriate.
Should NOT be: chatty, overly casual, slang-heavy, polished for effect, slogan-like, dramatic, rehearsed, corporate, academic, copywriter-y, LinkedIn-style, AI trying to imitate a person.

## Natural spoken language
Use contractions naturally: I'd, you're, we're, that's, doesn't, wouldn't. Prefer normal spoken vocabulary.
Good: "The first thing I'd look at is what happens after the lead comes in."
Not: "The first thing I would evaluate is your post-acquisition conversion infrastructure."
Good: "If you're already getting enough inquiries, more traffic may not be where I'd start."
Not: "Like, honestly, I wouldn't even worry about more leads right now."
The copy should sound spoken without relying on verbal filler.

## Avoid casual filler by default
Do NOT routinely use: like, honestly, I mean, okay, okay wait, kinda, basically, literally, you know, super, crazy, totally.
These can occasionally appear if they genuinely fit the established voice, but they are not default devices for making copy sound human.
Human does not mean casual. Human means the sentence follows the way a person naturally thinks and speaks.

## Use first-person judgment
Encouraged when it makes the copy more believable: "I'd look at...", "I'd want to know...", "I wouldn't increase spend yet.", "The first place I'd look is...", "Before changing the ads, I'd check...", "If this were my account, I'd...", "What I'd pay attention to is..."
These work because they sound like advice, not advertising. Do not force first person into every hook.

## Observations over declarations
Too ad-like: "Your marketing system is broken."
Better: "If leads are coming in but appointments are still inconsistent, there is probably something happening after the lead comes in that needs attention."
Too dramatic: "You're throwing money away on bad leads."
Better: "If a large percentage of your leads are never contacted or never book, increasing lead volume can make the numbers worse without fixing the underlying issue."

## Talk about what actually happens
Ground the idea in a recognizable business moment.
"Your agency can show you a strong cost per lead. But if nobody can tell you how many of those leads actually became treatment revenue, you still don't know whether the campaign is profitable."
"If the front desk is following up with new inquiries when they have time, I would look at that before assuming the ads need to change."
"A promotion can fill open appointments quickly. The part I'd pay attention to is what those patients do after the initial offer."
Do not invent a scene simply to make the copy vivid. Only use situations supported by the information provided or reasonably inherent to the business process.

## Let the thought breathe
Too compressed: "More leads won't fix broken follow-up."
Better: "If the leads you already have are not being followed up consistently, bringing in more of them is unlikely to solve the problem."
Too polished: "The gap between a lead and a patient is where revenue disappears."
Better: "Getting the lead is only the first step. You still need someone to contact them, book them, get them to show up, and ultimately convert them into a patient."
Plain is good when the thinking is good.

## Never
Clever endings, punchlines, slogans, neat reversals, forced metaphors, dramatic one-liners, manufactured controversy, fake provocations, rhetorical questions written only for effect, fake specificity, fake scenes, fake numbers, fake quotes, made-up offer details, em dashes, language designed primarily to sound quotable.
Avoid these structures as default devices: "X isn't the problem. Y is." / "It's not X. It's Y." / "You don't need X. You need Y." / "Here's the truth." / "The reality is..." / "What nobody tells you..." / "The secret is..." / "This changes everything." / "Most agencies..." / "Stop doing X." / "Imagine..." / "Picture this..."
A natural contrast is fine when that is genuinely the idea. Do not force every insight into a contrast formula.

## Do not manufacture direct response
Avoid constantly trying to create curiosity, shock the reader, challenge conventional wisdom, call out mistakes, manufacture pain.
Sometimes the strongest opening is simply a useful observation.
"If you're already spending consistently on marketing, I'd want to understand what happens between the lead coming in and the patient actually showing up before increasing the budget."

## Use the customer's world
Use the nouns, situations, decisions, and problems this customer actually encounters, in the terminology natural to the industry (consultation, treatment, provider capacity, front desk, lead follow-up, appointment, no-show, treatment revenue, ad spend, agency reporting).
Prefer concrete language over vague abstractions (growth, scale, optimization, success, results, transformation). Use abstract terms only when they are genuinely the clearest words.

## Different levels of directness
1. Observation: "A low cost per lead can look great in a report and still produce very little treatment revenue."
2. Expert judgment: "If your providers are already close to capacity, I would not automatically increase the ad budget."
3. Diagnosis: "When leads are coming in but appointments are inconsistent, I usually want to look at follow-up before changing the campaign."
4. Situation: "If you're getting plenty of inquiries but your team is still struggling to keep the calendar full, something is getting lost between the lead and the appointment."
5. Before-you-do-that: "Before putting more money into ads, I'd want to know how many of the leads you're already paying for are actually being contacted."
6. Clarification: "When someone says they have a lead quality problem, I'd want to know what that actually means. Are people not responding, not booking, not showing, or not buying?"
7. Outcome-led observation: "The goal is not simply to generate more inquiries. It's to generate patients who actually book, show up, and buy the treatments you want to grow."
Use these as ways of thinking, not rigid templates.

## Headlines
Slightly tighter than spoken hooks, but still something a human would say. Avoid slogan writing.
Too polished: "Turn Leads Into Loyal Patients" / Better: "What happens after the lead comes in matters just as much as the ad"
Too generic: "Get More High-Quality Patients" / Better: "How to tell whether your marketing is actually driving treatment revenue"
Clarity matters more than cleverness.

## Process
1. Identify the exact segment. 2. Identify the real situation. 3. Identify what the customer likely already understands. 4. Identify the useful observation or judgment. 5. Identify the relevant angle. 6. Identify any proof or factual claims that have actually been provided. 7. Write the idea in plain English first. 8. Turn it into natural spoken copy. 9. Remove unnecessary polish. 10. Remove casual filler. 11. Remove obvious copywriting devices. 12. Verify that every factual claim comes from information actually provided.
Then read the line aloud mentally. Ask: Would an experienced marketer actually say this to a client on a strategy call? Does it sound natural without relying on slang? Is the IDEA interesting, or is the wording trying to make it interesting? Could this have been written for almost any industry? Am I saying something useful? Am I inventing anything that was not provided? If the answer is wrong, rewrite it.

## Output per angle
5 conversational hooks, each a genuinely different entry point:
1. real situation / circumstance 2. diagnosis 3. expert judgment / what I'd examine 4. belief or instinct worth validating or reframing 5. before-you-do-that / decision point
Do not merely rewrite the same premise five ways.
3 headlines: clear, specific, concise, and human.
3 opening/body directions: each one short natural paragraph showing how the argument could continue. They should differ strategically (explain the mechanism / use available proof or a provided example / address the most relevant objection). Do not write three paraphrases.

The voice guide below was written for a marketer talking to a business owner. For these ads, switch the roles and keep every rule:
- The speaker is the business itself (the owner, provider or team), talking to a potential customer.
- The reader is that customer, not a business owner. Use the customer's world: their situation, their questions, their hesitations, the decision they're making.
